title: Privacy.
summary: Privacy information for An AUsome Life.
search: Site information · updated October 22, 2026Privacy.Useful tools, with clear choices about your words and pictures.The current websiteAn AUsome Life is a static website hosted through GitHub Pages. We do not operate visitor accounts, checkout, comments, a public upload gallery or an on-site contact form. We do not currently use our own advertising cookies or behavioral analytics.GitHub states that GitHub Pages logs visitors’ IP addresses for security. Read GitHub’s explanation. Page and image requests still reach the hosting provider even when a tool processes your input locally.Picture cards & visit plansWords typed into the picture-card and visit-plan editors and photos selected from your device are processed in the open browser tab. These tools do not send that text or those photos to us or an image provider, and they do not save your edited plan on our server. Save or print before closing or reloading.A saved PNG or PDF becomes a file on the device or in the destination you choose. The website cannot delete those copies. On a shared device, close the editing tab and consider where downloaded files and print jobs are kept.Public event or place links may prefill a plan using information in the link. URLs can appear in browser history and hosting logs, so do not put private names, care information or other sensitive details into a shared URL.Reading tools & your preferencesText size, color, spacing, motion and other reading choices apply in the current page without being sent to us. If you turn on “Remember my choices on this device,” those choices are saved in this browser’s local storage for other pages and later visits. We do not infer or ask for a disability or diagnosis. Uncheck the option or choose “Reset all choices” to remove the saved preferences. Leave it off on a shared device.Reading view prepares the visible page text in your browser. It leaves forms and editable inputs on the original page. Copying or printing sends the text only to the clipboard or print destination you choose.The reading-view “Read aloud” control lists only voices the browser identifies as local to the device. It does not send reading text to this website or request a remote voice. Voice availability and behavior depend on your browser and device. Listening starts when you choose it and stops when reading view is closed.Open reading tools and helpImage prompts & future generationThe image-prompt helper prepares text for you to copy. “Copy prompt & open ChatGPT” places that text on your clipboard and opens ChatGPT; it does not submit your prompt. If you paste it into a separate AI service, that service’s privacy and retention terms apply. Use a general description when a person’s name, diagnosis or private address is unnecessary.This site does not currently research or generate a new image live for a visitor. Before a live service is introduced, we will explain what is sent, which providers process it, how long it is retained and what choices you have. Your local photos will not be silently sent as references.External services & contactOpening a map, retailer, social account or video preview takes you to another service. An activated video player may load content from that provider. Those services have their own privacy practices. Other spoken-content tools you choose outside this website follow your browser or operating system’s settings and privacy practices.If you email us, the email providers process the information you choose to send. We use it to respond and address the matter raised. Please leave private care records and unnecessary identifying details out of an initial message.Questions or privacy concerns? Contact the editor. This page will be updated when the site’s data practices change.Your browser, your choiceSafari and other browsers sometimes show their own notices about privacy protections. Those messages come from the browser, not from An AUsome Life. You do not need to lower your browser’s privacy settings to read our stories. If a page or tool is not working as expected, please tell us so we can investigate.

title: A Little Camelot in Boston
summary: With Mom-Mom at Boston’s April 2026 Profound Autism Summit: Governor Healey’s moving caregiving speech, wonderful questions, music, practical resources, and the 2027 dates.
search: Boston, Massachusetts · April 2026A Little Camelot in BostonWith Mom-Mom at the Profound Autism Summit: wonderful questions, music, a few tears, and a rare world arranged around helping us care for the people we love.An AUsome Life · A reflection on April 16–17, 2026A moment of connection at the April 2026 Profound Autism Summit. Some rooms ask you to begin with an explanation. Before you can ask your question, you have to explain your child. What support looks like in your family. Why an apparently simple suggestion might be complicated. How much you love someone whose needs do not fit neatly into the systems around him. At the Profound Autism Summit in Boston this April, I felt the relief of entering a room where so much of that was already understood. I went with my mother: James’s grandmother, our beloved Mom-Mom. The April 16–17, 2026 gathering at the Hilton Boston Park Plaza brought together people working to improve life for autistic people with substantial, ongoing support needs. We arrived as a mother and a grandmother, with the person we both love at the center of our reasons for being there. And for a little while, the world seemed arranged around helping us care for him. A little Camelot Camelot is the word I keep coming back to. For those days, the annual summit offers a rare world where the questions that occupy so much of our lives belong on the main stage. Communication. Safety. Adulthood. The ordinary, enormous work of helping someone have a good day and imagining how to make a good life possible. The difficulties do not disappear when we walk into a conference. But there is something restorative about finding a place where understanding them is a shared undertaking. Where people have gathered to think carefully, exchange what they know, and ask what could be better. There is room to learn. There is also room to exhale. Having my mother there made that feeling more personal. James is my son and her grandson. We love him from different places in the same family, and here we were, learning together. There is comfort in hearing something useful beside a person who already knows who you are thinking about. For a little while, the world seemed arranged around helping us care for the people we love. It began with someone they loved Behind the organizations that made this gathering possible are families who wanted more for someone they loved. Liz Martineau founded Nashoba Learning Group in 2002, inspired by her son with profound autism. That beginning matters to me: a mother taking what she knew about her child’s needs and helping build something that could serve other families, too. The Profound Autism Alliance, founded in 2023, grew from the Ursitti family’s experience. Cofounders Judith and Amy Ursitti brought a mother’s and a sister’s love for Jack to that work. Jack is himself named a cofounder and the organization’s Chief Inspiration Officer. Nashoba Learning Group created the summit in collaboration with the Profound Autism Alliance. Their work gives that deeply personal love a wider reach: more people to learn from, more questions to ask, more families who might find help. I felt that connection sitting beside my mother. We had come because we love James. So much of what surrounded us had begun with that same impulse: love for a child, a sibling, a person whose future matters. A Norwegian connection, courtesy of a sweater Then there was a small, lovely moment that had nothing to do with a presentation slide. A fellow Norwegian found my mother and me because I was wearing one of my favorite sweaters—a Dale of Norway. I love that a sweater could do that. In the middle of a gathering organized around one kind of shared experience, it opened the door to another. A familiar pattern, a little recognition, and suddenly a room full of people felt more connected. That belongs in my memory of the summit, too. Alongside the important information were the human details: my mother beside me, the people we met, and the unexpected ways we found one another. The wonderful questions I loved the questions. A thoughtful question can hold so much knowledge: what someone has already tried, what they have noticed, what still does not make sense, and what they hope might be possible for a person they love or support. Listening to those wonderful questions was part of the education. They brought the conversation close to daily life, where an idea has to work for an actual person, in an actual family, on an ordinary afternoon. The questions I carry into a gathering like this are very practical. How can we make it easier for James to tell us what he wants? How can we support his love of water while taking safety seriously? What helps him participate, make choices, and enjoy more of the world? How do we plan for adulthood while continuing to notice the life he is living now? A room that welcomes detailed, complicated questions gives us somewhere to begin. People, music, and the pleasure of being together At least a few profoundly autistic people attended, too. Their presence mattered. I want gatherings about support to make room for the people receiving it—to be there, to take part, and to have their own experience of the day. And the Flutie performers were absolute superstars. Their performance was amazing, one of the joyful memories I brought home. The Doug Flutie, Jr. Foundation for Autism helps make space for autistic artists and performers; at the summit, we got to enjoy the music and the people making it. There was so much serious work to consider, and there was also room for pleasure. I loved that. A good life needs both the right support and things worth getting together for. Ideas with a place in everyday life The photographs I brought home remind me how much of the learning concerned the texture of an ordinary day. One slide celebrated diversity in communication. Others explored picture communication, communication buttons, and AAC—augmentative and alternative communication. For me, the point is deeply personal: making more room for James to express himself, and helping the people around him become better listeners. I want his preferences to shape his life. His yes matters. His no matters. The things that delight him matter. Support should give those things more room. A reminder from the summit: communication can take many forms, and individual preferences deserve respect. There were Swim Angelfish visual supports for swimming, too, and an Inclusive Fitness presentation connecting physical strength with everyday actions: standing up, navigating a curb, carrying something, reaching a shelf. I appreciated the attention to the small details that can make participation easier. Visual supports and access to swimming.Movement connected with everyday life. Slide: Inclusive Fitness. Another slide described a family AAC camp at Zeno Mountain Farm, with activities built around autistic participants’ interests. The list included dancing, movies, karaoke, sledding, and s’mores. Even in a photograph of a conference screen, there was the lovely outline of a life: people having things to look forward to, together. A family AAC camp, and a list full of things to look forward to. The Lurie Center for Autism booth was especially informative. I appreciated having a place to stop, learn, and find out more. Useful information is easier to carry home when there is someone there to help you make sense of it. The center’s website also offers links to family education and resources for continuing that learning. That is part of what I mean by a world designed to help us care. Care includes access to pleasure, friendship, movement, and belonging. It includes the opportunity to try something because it might be fun. Governor Healey, and a future worth planning for Governor Maura Healey’s speech about caregiving brought a tear—or more—to my eyes. Hearing her speak, with my mother beside me, I felt how much it means for the work of caring to be recognized. So much of it happens quietly: the planning, the learning, the trying again, the love running through an ordinary day. It was moving to hear caregiving receive that kind of public attention. For anyone who would like to hear her remarks, the Profound Autism Alliance’s Massachusetts page links to the governor’s summit speech. Just weeks earlier, on March 23, she had signed Executive Order No. 656, establishing a framework for a statewide strategy to support adults with profound autism. The order calls for coordination across state systems and an advisory council to help shape that work. The state’s announcement explains the March 23 action. For a family thinking about a child’s future, that attention matters. Our children grow up. Their lives continue to deserve planning, investment, understanding, and people prepared to support them well. An executive order is a beginning. Its promise will matter most in the everyday lives of the people it is intended to serve. Still, it was meaningful to be there with my mother, at a gathering where that future was being taken seriously. A date for our next little Camelot The 2027 Profound Autism Summit is scheduled for April 15–16 at the Hilton Boston Park Plaza. I am glad there is another gathering to look toward. For families considering it, the official summit page is the place to follow announcements and check current registration details. Ask the organizers about participation needs and any available financial assistance. Getting away to learn can take considerable arranging when you are a caregiver; that part of the planning matters, too. In the meantime, the 2026 program and recording information and ProfoundVillage offer ways to keep learning between gatherings. What I want to bring home For me, naming substantial support needs belongs alongside respecting the full person: their communication, preferences, relationships, rights, and capacity to keep learning. I want a future shaped with autistic people, including people who need extensive support to participate and be heard. I want caregivers to have help, and I want the people we care for to have as much say as possible in their own lives. Those hopes belong together. That is what I want to carry out of our little Camelot. The summit gives us a brief experience of a world where people have come prepared to help. Each year, it makes room for questions that can be difficult to find room for elsewhere. It allows families to imagine what more consistent understanding could feel like. I went with Mom-Mom, wearing a sweater that helped a fellow Norwegian find us. I came away with ideas, wonderful questions, photographs, music in my memory, and a few tears I was glad to have shed. Above all, I remember being among people who understood why we were there. And I keep thinking about how lovely it would be to make more of the world feel like that. A place where our loved ones belong, and where helping them live well is something we do together. Keep learningThe 2026 summit page links to its program and session recordings. The organizers say 2026 attendees retain access to recordings, with purchase options for others. Photographs from our summit collection. Presentation slides remain the work of their respective presenters. The questions I describe as my own are reflections, rather than quotations from other attendees. title: A little lake time.
summary: Fall foliage, lakeside boats and a rainbow: a lovely Rangeley, Maine getaway from our family's photo album, with practical notes for planning a visit.
search: The journalRangeley, MaineA grandparents’ field note The rainbow rather stole the show. From the family camera roll, Rangeley, Maine. Fall in the western Maine mountainsA little lake time.The grandparents, some downtime in Rangeley, and a very good reason to stop looking at the clock.October 6, 2026Mom-Mom & Grandpa Steve (aka Grandma & Grandpa) got a little time away in Maine. The photographs have all the ingredients I love: fall color, boats at the dock, a dog by the water, and a sky doing something magnificent.Grandparents deserve a chapter like this, too. From their corner of the lakeA day with room around it.There is something especially lovely about seeing the grandparents get a bit of downtime. We have plenty of family stories with a destination, a departure time, and several people’s needs to fit into the day. This little Rangeley chapter gets to be about a pause.Look at that shoreline: the boats tucked along the docks, the hills turning gold and rust, the ducks gathered near the grass. In one photograph, dark clouds sit above the village and a rainbow lands almost neatly behind it. Maine has apparently decided to handle the decorations.I love the ordinary part just as much. A jacket, a dog on a lead, a few minutes by the water. The sort of scene you might walk past while trying to get somewhere else—and then realize it was the thing you wanted all along. A little company at the water’s edge. The ducks appear to have called a meeting. A lakeside pause. Original editorial illustration inspired by a Maine landscape, not a map of the visit.The good partLet the view be the outing.A beautiful place does not need a very ambitious plan. For a grandparent getaway—or anyone whose idea of a holiday includes sitting down—I like the thought of choosing one lovely place and leaving time to enjoy it.A lake view can be the whole afternoon.That is the feeling I want to keep from these photographs: a little breathing room, a little fall color, and the people we love getting a turn to enjoy both.A broad sky, a patch of sunshine, and plenty to look at. The family photographs above show the grandparents’ getaway; the places below have their own facilities and access conditions.Open the Rangeley mapThe map is for regional orientation. Check the route from parking to your chosen seat, viewpoint or restroom with the site operator. For a lakeside picnicRangeley Lake State Park. Maine lists day-use parking, restrooms and picnic tables as accessible; the picnic area as generally accessible; the beach as accessible with assistance; and the trails as not accessible. Ask staff which route best fits your needs.The published day-use season is May 1–October 15, 9 a.m. to sunset. Off-season facilities close and entry is on foot from outside the gate, which changes the outing considerably.Park information & current notices · Official access ratings In-season questions: 207-864-3858 For the view, with less walkingQuill Hill. The operator describes a four-mile dirt road to the summit, parking at the top and panoramic views. That makes it an option to investigate when a mountain hike is not the plan. Ask about the surface between parking and the viewpoint, seating, and restroom arrangements.The site’s seasonal notices vary between “through October” and “mid-October.” Confirm the gate is open before setting out; cars, motorcycles and ATVs also use the road.Quill Hill updates · Official directions For a gentle wander, if it suitsHatchery Brook Preserve. Rangeley Lakes Heritage Trust describes easy walking near the village, waterfront picnic spots and stretches of bog bridging. “Easy” does not establish wheelchair access: ask about widths, transitions, wet surfaces and the distance to a comfortable turning point.Preserve details & trail map Trail questions: 207-864-7311 The useful detailsMake the pause comfortable. Look beyond “waterfront.”For a stay, ask for the actual route from the car to the room and the lake view. Check steps, slopes, firm surfaces, bathroom layout, bed height and a place to sit with a backrest. The grassy slope and shoreline rocks visible in these photos are a useful reminder that a lovely view and an easy route are separate questions. Plan for sound, light and weather.Open water can mean wind, glare and boat noise; a scenic overlook can bring engines and conversation. Ask when a place tends to be quieter, bring familiar sensory supports if useful, and choose a stop with an easy return to shelter. A photograph cannot tell us how quiet a place felt. Keep the water’s edge optional.Enjoying a lake need not involve a dock or a boat. Choose a stable place to sit back from the edge. If close supervision around water is part of your family’s routine, build that into the plan. For a boat outing, ask separately about boarding, transfers and suitable life jackets. Give the dog—and the ducks—space.Check pet rules for the specific property and outing. Keep your dog close on a lead, leave wildlife room, and watch the ducks without feeding them. A pet-friendly listing is also worth checking for room restrictions and fees before booking. Before you leaveThe small, sensible list.Choose one main stop and confirm its seasonal opening.Check parking, the walking or rolling surface, a seat and an open restroom.Bring a warm layer, rain protection, water and something familiar to eat.Save directions before setting out and keep the return plan simple.Leave enough room in the day to stay a little longer—or finish early. For this field note, I keep coming back to the rainbow. The grandparents got their lake time, and we got these photographs to enjoy. A very good little chapter.Family photographs supplied for this story. Regional planning information checked October 6, 2026 against the linked official sources. title: A little stop. A lot of spring.
summary: A must-do Rhode Island spring stop: Rose Shack in Saunderstown for a host or mother-in-law gift and a family photograph among the flowers.
search: The journalSaunderstown, Rhode IslandFrom the spring family album · October 19, 2026 Rose Shack · A Rhode Island spring favoriteA little stop. A lot of spring.One for your Rhode Island spring list: flowers for a host, a gift for your mother-in-law, and a photograph worth keeping.Some stops deserve a place in the family album as well as the shopping bag.James and Michael, spring flowers, and a photograph I am very glad we took. From an earlier family visit. Put it on the spring list.Yellow tulips. Pink and white hyacinths. A little shed with FLOWERS across the roof. Our photograph from Rose Shack in Saunderstown has the sort of color that makes you forget how recently you were scraping the windshield.And there are James and Michael in the middle of it. James was smaller then; the smile is the part I keep coming back to.For us, this is a must-do Rhode Island stop in spring. Come for something growing, leave with a present, and take a photograph while you are there. It need not become an entire day's itinerary.A gift that looks like spring.Heading to somebody's house? Looking for a gift for your mother-in-law? This is exactly the sort of place I would put on the list. Choose a flowering plant that suits the recipient's space and gardening ambitions. title: A little research, a short car ride.
summary: A surprise Shaker history day in Harvard, Massachusetts: a thoughtful, inexpensive family gift, local history, and the craftsmanship behind Shaker furniture.
search: Harvard, Massachusetts · From the family albumA little research, a short car ride.Michael’s surprise Shaker history day: a thoughtful gift close to home, with James along for the adventure.Published October 22, 2026A family moment at Harvard’s Shaker burial ground. A little research, a short car ride, and a day planned around something I love. Such a thoughtful gift. ❤️ Michael surprised me with a Shaker history day in Harvard, Massachusetts, with James along for the adventure. I grew up right nearby, and despite being a history buff, I’d somehow never taken the time to explore this part of our local history. Apparently, I needed someone to turn “we should do that someday” into an actual plan. 😂 Harvard was home to the first Shaker community in Massachusetts, with roots going back to Mother Ann Lee’s visit in 1781. The remaining buildings and burial ground are reminders of a community that once farmed, worked, and worshipped here. The National Park Service tells more of the village’s story. My mother, Mom-Mom, has always loved Shaker furniture. Growing up, we’d make special trips to furniture stores in Gardner and Lancaster to buy pieces. That love of simple, beautifully made furniture was part of my childhood, so this day had a lovely connection to those memories, too. And then there’s the furniture. Those simple wooden chairs, beautiful cupboards, and carefully made tables reflect the Shakers’ beliefs about simplicity, usefulness, and craftsmanship. Even the familiar ladder-back chairs have a story beyond their appearance: they were practical objects made with extraordinary care. The Metropolitan Museum of Art explores that connection between belief and design.Original editorial illustration · the simple beauty of Shaker chairs. I love learning about the everyday details of people’s lives—what they made, how they lived, and what mattered to them. Getting to explore those stories so close to where I grew up, with my own family, made the day especially meaningful. It cost very little. The gift was the thought, the research, and having someone else take care of the planning. When you spend so much time organizing family life and caregiving, that part feels especially good. Thank you, Michael, for remembering the history-loving part of me and making a day of it. ❤️ A little history close to homeFor the background and a map of the historic village, start with the Harvard Historical Society’s Shaker history guide. It connects the surviving buildings, burial ground, and Holy Hill with the larger story of the community.For your own thoughtful outing gift, choose a subject your person loves, research a few nearby stops, and take care of the plan.
